CARES Architecture Decision Package

Status: Proposed architecture preparation; not implemented; not tested.

This package resolves the design gaps identified in the repository documentation. It is a decision record, not a database or application implementation. Mandatory CARES requirements are not changed.

Status labels

  • EXISTING APPROVED REQUIREMENT: established by the project owner or mandatory master instruction.
  • EXISTING PROPOSAL: already proposed in the repository documentation.
  • NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION: a recommendation added by this package.
  • OWNER DECISION REQUIRED: cannot be made without project-owner approval.
  • NOT IMPLEMENTED: no corresponding working implementation exists.
  • NOT TESTED: no end-to-end or PostgreSQL verification exists.

1. Executive summary

The repository has a clear identity and licensing requirement but no implementation evidence:

  • PostgreSQL is mandatory, but there is no PostgreSQL integration.
  • The one-device/one-licensed-asset requirement is mandatory.
  • A data source is a collection channel or credentialed connector instance, not a device.
  • One data source may report many devices.
  • One device may receive data from many data sources.
  • A canonical CARES asset represents one physical or logical monitored device.
  • The current prototype is process-local and cannot enforce quota or identity atomically.

This package recommends:

  1. Represent source-device identity as a source_device_binding plus one or more versioned fingerprint aliases.
  2. Recalculate a source-device fingerprint only through an audited migration run.
  3. Never derive canonical asset identity from the fingerprint.
  4. Serialize registration per tenant with the PostgreSQL tenant quota row.
  5. Use tenant-scoped identity uniqueness and a stable canonical asset ID.
  6. Keep 30-day deactivation grace and pending-identity quota reservation as owner decisions.
  7. Keep the original ten-phase roadmap as the approved baseline.
  8. Treat the revised roadmap and all cross-platform destinations as proposals.

PostgreSQL implementation readiness: NOT READY FOR FULL SCHEMA IMPLEMENTATION. Core tenant, identity and quota structures need owner decisions and formal schema review first. Read-only tenant/admin tables may be specified later, but asset, source binding and licensing migrations should not begin until the unresolved lifecycle and fingerprint-rotation decisions are closed.

2. Current architectural gaps

Confirmed gaps

Gap State Risk
PostgreSQL integration NOT IMPLEMENTED No persistence or database uniqueness
Tenant RLS and trusted tenant context NOT DESIGNED Cross-tenant writes or reads
Canonical asset identity EXISTING PROPOSAL Duplicate or false device merge
Source-device identity EXISTING PROPOSAL Connector-wide IDs may be mistaken for device IDs
Fingerprint key rotation NEEDS DESIGN CLARIFICATION Interrupted or concurrent migration
Atomic quota EXISTING PROPOSAL Concurrent registration may oversubscribe
Merge/split EXISTING PROPOSAL Licensing and event lineage corruption
Lifecycle/grace OWNER DECISION REQUIRED Billing ambiguity
Cross-platform roadmap OWNER DECISION REQUIRED No revised destination for BSD, macOS, Android or iOS

Remaining contradictions

  • The revised roadmap does not assign a destination to BSD, macOS, Android or iOS development.
  • The existing data model says source-device identifiers are namespaced and fingerprinted, but it does not specify the exact overlap state machine or migration resume protocol.
  • The 30-day grace and pending reservations are sometimes presented as technical defaults. They remain commercial policy proposals.

3. Workstream A: source-device fingerprint rotation

3.1 Identity model

Existing approved requirement

Each unique monitored device is exactly one licensed asset. Different data sources may report the same device. A data source is not itself an asset.

Existing proposed tuple

(tenant_id, data_source_id, protected_source_device_key_fingerprint)

New technical recommendation

Use two related representations:

  1. A canonical source_device_binding representing the stable relationship between one source, one source-local device key and one CARES asset.
  2. A versioned source_device_fingerprint_alias representing each fingerprint used to discover that binding.
flowchart LR
  R["Raw source-device identifier"] -->|protect| F["Fingerprint alias"]
  F -->|same binding| B["Source-device binding"]
  B --> A["Canonical CARES asset"]
  DS["Data source / connector instance"] --> B

The raw identifier is not the canonical identity. It is not used as a PostgreSQL uniqueness key. The canonical asset UUID is not derived from the fingerprint.

3.2 Proposed data model

CREATE TABLE fingerprint_key (
    tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
    key_version bigint NOT NULL,
    algorithm text NOT NULL,
    scope text NOT NULL,
    secret_ref text NOT NULL,
    state text NOT NULL,
    activated_at timestamptz,
    retire_after timestamptz,
    retired_at timestamptz,
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, key_version),
    CONSTRAINT fingerprint_key_state CHECK (
        state IN ('draft', 'active', 'overlap', 'retiring', 'retired')
    )
);

CREATE TABLE source_device_binding (
    tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
    binding_id uuid NOT NULL,
    data_source_id uuid NOT NULL,
    canonical_asset_id uuid NOT NULL,
    source_device_key_id uuid NOT NULL,
    state text NOT NULL,
    first_seen_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
    last_seen_at timestamptz,
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, binding_id),
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, data_source_id, source_device_key_id),
    CONSTRAINT source_device_binding_state CHECK (
        state IN ('pending', 'active', 'inactive', 'merged', 'removed')
    )
);

CREATE TABLE source_device_fingerprint_alias (
    tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
    data_source_id uuid NOT NULL,
    fingerprint_digest bytea NOT NULL,
    algorithm text NOT NULL,
    key_version bigint NOT NULL,
    binding_id uuid NOT NULL,
    state text NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
    last_seen_at timestamptz,
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, data_source_id, fingerprint_digest),
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, data_source_id, fingerprint_digest),
    CONSTRAINT fingerprint_alias_state CHECK (
        state IN ('active', 'overlap', 'deprecated', 'retired')
    )
);

CREATE TABLE fingerprint_rotation_run (
    tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
    run_id uuid NOT NULL,
    old_key_version bigint NOT NULL,
    new_key_version bigint NOT NULL,
    algorithm text NOT NULL,
    status text NOT NULL,
    last_binding_id uuid,
    last_seen_at timestamptz,
    processed_count bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    conflict_count bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    verification_status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'not_started',
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, run_id),
    CONSTRAINT rotation_status CHECK (
        status IN ('authorized', 'running', 'paused', 'verifying', 'completed',
                   'failed', 'cancelled')
    )
);

The examples omit tenant foreign keys in their shortened form. A complete implementation must include tenant-aware foreign keys for data_source_id, canonical_asset_id, and binding_id. The exact SQL representation must be reviewed by PostgreSQL and security engineers before migration creation.

NOT IMPLEMENTED: these example structures are design proposals, not schema.

3.3 Fingerprint key scope and custody

NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION:

  • Use HMAC-SHA-256 or a stronger approved keyed digest.
  • Use a separate HMAC key for each tenant or for the platform with a tenant-scoped key derivation context.
  • Store key material in a secret manager or KMS-backed envelope.
  • Store only secret references and key metadata in PostgreSQL.
  • Never log raw source identifiers or HMAC keys.
  • Require two-person approval for key activation and retirement where platform policy requires it.
  • Record actor, run ID, old/new key version, algorithm, activation time and retirement time.

The exact key scope is OWNER DECISION REQUIRED. Tenants need stronger separation, but global key rotation is easier operationally. The recommended default is tenant-derived/platform-managed keys, subject to security and tenancy review.

3.4 Initial source-device identification

Initial registration pseudocode:

begin tenant transaction
  authenticate data_source_id
  resolve tenant_id from trusted source credential
  normalize raw source_device_key
  load current fingerprint key (active or overlap)
  digest = keyedFingerprint(raw, algorithm, key_version)

  find aliases for:
    exact (tenant_id, data_source_id, digest)
    and, if migration overlap is active,
    possible old-key aliases associated with source_device_key_id

  if exactly one alias and it points to one binding:
      lock binding
      lock canonical asset
      mark alias last_seen
      add no asset usage
      commit

  if multiple aliases point to the same binding:
      use that binding
      add no asset usage
      record alias convergence
      commit

  if aliases point to different bindings:
      create pending identity conflict
      quarantine data
      add no usage
      commit for review

  if no alias exists:
      evaluate existing authoritative, namespace-specific identity claims
      if exactly one asset match:
          lock tenant license row
          create binding
          create fingerprint alias
          add no usage
          commit
      else if no strong match:
          lock tenant license row
          recheck quota and alias uniqueness
          if quota available:
              create canonical asset
              create binding
              create fingerprint alias
              append lifecycle/license records
              increment usage
          else reject or create pending case according to owner policy
commit

The no-alias branch must never derive canonical identity from hostname, IP address or weak similarity.

3.5 Overlap representation

The overlap has these states:

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> OldActive
  OldActive --> Overlap: authorize key rotation
  Overlap --> NewActive: old key registered aliases verified
  NewActive --> RetiringOld: overlap grace complete
  RetiringOld --> RetiredOld: verification and removal complete
  RetiredOld --> [*]

During overlap:

  • The old key remains usable.
  • The new key is installed.
  • Registration may produce either fingerprint.
  • Both aliases reference the same binding_id.
  • Both aliases remain linked to the same canonical asset.
  • The unique triple is enforced independently for each (tenant_id, data_source_id, fingerprint_digest).
  • The old and new fingerprint rows do not create or increment a usage counter.

The exact tuple for lookup is always:

(tenant_id, data_source_id, protected_source_device_key_fingerprint)

The application never compares raw identifiers as database keys.

3.6 Lookup during overlap

Lookup order:

  1. Calculate the presented fingerprint with the provided or negotiated key version.
  2. Search exact (tenant_id, data_source_id, fingerprint_digest).
  3. If exactly one alias resolves, lock and use its binding_id.
  4. If no alias matches but a current raw identifier or a stable source key exists, verify it against existing aliases through an authorized, audited migration/identity service.
  5. If two aliases resolve to the same binding, continue with no usage change.
  6. If aliases resolve to different bindings, enter conflict quarantine.

The application must not silently choose one asset based on a different raw value or weak similarity.

3.7 Rotation transaction boundaries

One rotation run is not one long transaction across all tenants. Use small tenant-scoped batches.

One batch transaction must contain:

  • Migration run and batch checkpoint.
  • Locked binding or range of bindings.
  • One new alias per binding if it does not exist.
  • Conflict and verification status.
  • No asset, license counter or canonical identity modifications for successful rows.

The batch pseudocode:

begin transaction
  lock migration run row
  verify run state is running
  load next binding batch after last_binding_id
  for each binding:
      lock binding
      find all old aliases
      for each old alias:
          derive new digest from protected source identifier
          insert new alias only if absent
          if new digest already belongs to another binding:
              mark conflict
              do not merge assets
          else attach new alias to original binding
          mark old alias overlap or deprecated according to policy
  update run checkpoint and counters
  append rotation audit event
commit

3.8 Batch idempotency

Use:

(tenant_id, run_id, binding_id)

as the batch item key.

If the batch is retried:

  • Existing aliases are a no-op.
  • Existing checkpoints remain valid.
  • No asset or usage record is added.
  • Conflict state is preserved and reported.
  • The batch item cannot advance past an unresolved conflict.

The migration run must not advance to complete while unresolved conflicts remain.

3.9 Crash and interruption recovery

The migration state is persisted on every batch:

  • last_binding_id
  • processed count
  • conflict count
  • checkpoint time
  • verification status

After application or PostgreSQL restart:

  1. Load the run by run_id.
  2. Lock the run row.
  3. Resume after the last committed checkpoint.
  4. Re-evaluate all rows in the next batch.
  5. Use database uniqueness and idempotency keys to prevent duplicate aliases.
  6. Never restart by recounting assets or allocating quota again.

If PostgreSQL commits the checkpoint but returns an application timeout, re-run the next batch. PostgreSQL row uniqueness and binding identity prevent duplicate work.

3.10 Duplicate prevention

Duplicate assets and usage are prevented by:

  • One canonical asset UUID.
  • Transactional tenant quota locking.
  • Stable binding_id and source_device_key_id.
  • Unique source-device alias triples.
  • Identity re-check inside the migration/registration transaction.
  • No asset or usage write for successful fingerprint aliases.
  • No retry allocation without the original idempotency key.
  • Conflict state instead of weighted or automatic merge.

If a new fingerprint already exists and points to a different binding, do not create an asset or merge assets. The migration stops at a conflict and requires reviewed resolution.

3.11 Retirement

Old key retirement must occur only after:

  • Both old and new key aliases are present.
  • Registration traffic proves new fingerprint lookup.
  • Verification confirms every binding has exactly one canonical asset.
  • Conflict count is zero.
  • Owner-defined overlap period is complete.
  • New key secrets are operational and backed up.

Retirement transaction:

  • Mark old aliases deprecated.
  • Verify no registration is using the old key.
  • Mark old key retiring.
  • After retention expiry, mark aliases retired.
  • Revoke old key material.
  • Record retention and deletion evidence.

Keeping an old fingerprint row after key retirement must not allow an old key to be used. The row may remain only for audit or deterministic lookup according to policy.

3.12 Concurrency and races

Registration and migration may occur concurrently.

Required rules:

  • Migration inserts aliases, never canonical assets.
  • Registration locks the binding before alias updates.
  • A tenant row is locked for every possible new asset or quota state change.
  • Both old and new aliases reference the same binding through no-merge invariants.
  • Alias uniqueness is checked under PostgreSQL constraints.
  • Split/merge operations lock canonical assets in deterministic UUID order.
  • Migration workers cannot advance past unresolved conflicts.

3.13 Verification and rollback

Verification must establish:

  • Every overlap alias has exactly one binding.
  • Every binding is linked to exactly one canonical asset.
  • No canonical asset has a duplicate active source-device binding in a conflict state.
  • The tenant usage counter equals active/approved billable states.
  • No migration batch changed licensed usage.
  • Old and new aliases agree on the same canonical asset.

Rollback strategy:

  • Before key retirement, migration can stop and remain in overlap.
  • Registration can continue on the old key.
  • New aliases can be marked deprecated and removed only by audited migration.
  • The canonical assets and license counters are not rolled back merely to undo key migration.
  • Materialized key retirement is irreversible; key retirement must follow successful verification.

3.14 Security risks

  • Fingerprint collision or weak HMAC configuration.
  • Key access by migration workers.
  • Tenant cross-key reuse.
  • Raw identifier exposure.
  • Migration conflict that conceals two devices.
  • Premature key retirement.
  • Migration worker operating before tenant authorization.
  • Lookups trusting payload-provided key versions.
  • Duplicate aliases or bindings caused by missing tenant-inclusive constraints.

3.15 Missing requirements

Before implementation is sufficient, define:

  • Key scope by tenant/platform.
  • Exact HMAC algorithm and key derivation.
  • Fingerprint key rotation overlap length.
  • Old-fingerprint grace behavior.
  • Conflict approval workflow.
  • Lookup behavior if old and new aliases disagree.
  • Migration retry and batch-size policy.
  • Key retirement retention and audit.

NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION: migration should be asynchronous, resumable and tenant-scoped. It should not alter canonical assets or quota counts.

4. Workstream B: asset licensing lifecycle

4.1 Technical invariant and commercial boundary

EXISTING APPROVED REQUIREMENT: exactly one licensed asset for every unique monitored device; all data sources are distinct from that licensed asset.

NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION: each lifecycle transition must be transactional and update the canonical asset, source bindings, license usage and lifecycle history together.

4.2 Lifecycle state table

State Canonical record exists Active asset count Reserved slot Incoming data Authorization Audit
Pending identity resolution Proposed yes: canonical UUID may exist as pending; owner policy decides whether provisional/hidden No, proposed Proposed one slot, owner decision Quarantine or reject; no normal analysis Customer or administrator may be required to resolve Conflict, source, evidence, policy and expiration
Active Yes Yes, exactly one No extra reservation Accepted and processed Source credential authorized Seen/source binding/event/license
Inactive/offline Yes Technical policy decides if still active Usually none, owner decision Accepted if source credential remains valid; may buffer No state change solely due timeout Last-seen, heartbeats, offline transition
Deactivated Yes, tombstone or lifecycle record No, proposed Proposed 30-day grace slot, owner decision Reject normal source data or keep quarantine Customer or administrator authorization, owner approval for policy Deactivation reason, actor, source revocation and timestamp
Reserved Yes/tombstone No, unless owner defines billable Yes Reactivate or reject according to grace state Customer or administrator, owner policy Reservation/release and expiry
Reactivated Yes Yes, exactly one Release reservation within transaction Accepted Customer or authorized administrator Reuse canonical ID and source/license history
Permanently removed Tombstone/history recommended No No, unless owner exception Reject Permanent removal authorization owner decision Removal actor, reason, deactivation source, tombstone
Merged Survivor and tombstone for losing asset Survivor one; losing no usage No new billable asset Redirect source bindings to survivor; no duplicate Privileged authorized merge Before/after, alias/source transfer, usage delta
Split Survivor plus new canonical asset Survivor and new asset after verification One additional slot must be available Split source bindings and quarantine ambiguous data Privileged authorized split Before/after, source mapping and usage delta

4.3 State transitions

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> PendingIdentity: ambiguous or missing identity
  PendingIdentity --> Active: identity verified and quota available
  PendingIdentity --> [*]: rejected or expired
  [*] --> Active: authoritative first registration
  Active --> InactiveOffline: no heartbeat / timeout
  InactiveOffline --> Active: data or heartbeat resumes
  InactiveOffline --> Deactivated: last source revoked or policy
  Active --> Deactivated: last active source revoked
  Deactivated --> Reserved: owner-approved grace policy
  Reserved --> Reactivated: authorized source reconnect
  Reserved --> PermanentlyRemoved: grace expiry or owner approval
  Deactivated --> PermanentlyRemoved: immediate removal policy
  Reactivated --> Active: registration accepted
  Active --> Merged: reviewed merge
  Merged --> Active: survivor continues
  Active --> Split: reviewed split
  Split --> Active: both canonical assets active

The diagram intentionally leaves commercial grace and reservation behavior as proposals.

4.4 Transition requirements

Pending identity resolution

  • Canonical asset record may exist as pending only if it is explicitly not billable.
  • Incoming payload should be quarantined or rejected. It must not enter normal detection as confirmed attribution.
  • A pending case may reserve quota, but this remains OWNER DECISION REQUIRED.
  • Resolution to an existing asset releases the reservation.
  • Resolution to a new device atomically creates one active asset and increments usage.

Active

  • Has at least one active source binding.
  • Counts as exactly one asset.
  • Source attachment does not increase usage.
  • Quota lock and uniqueness are required for first registration.

Inactive/offline

  • Canonical asset and source credentials remain.
  • It must not be removed or deactivated merely because a heartbeat is missed.
  • Timeouts require offline policy and last-seen records.
  • It may remain active billable until a separate lifecycle transition.

Deactivated

  • No active source binding is accepted.
  • It should not be considered a unique currently monitored device by default.
  • 30-day grace is PROPOSED — OWNER APPRO APPROVAL REQUIRED.
  • Reserving quota is OWNER DECISION REQUIRED.

Reserved

  • The canonical record/tombstone remains.
  • It may reserve capacity separately from billable count, if owner policy approves.
  • Incoming source data may reactivate only through authorized re-enrollment or owner-approved process.

Reactivated

  • Reuse the canonical UUID during grace.
  • Convert reservation to active in the same transaction.
  • Add no usage increment if already counted as active? The implementation must define this explicitly. During grace, a reserved slot should not be treated as both billable and reserved.

Permanently removed

  • Requires explicit permanent-removal authorization according to owner policy.
  • Preserve tombstone and licensing history when required.
  • Raw event retention is separate from asset licensing.
  • A later re-enrollment after removal must pass current quota and identity rules.

Merged

  • Exactly one canonical asset survives.
  • Losing asset becomes merged/tombstone.
  • Source bindings move under constraints.
  • Licensed count decreases only after verifying two assets represent one device.
  • Event lineage must preserve the original canonical IDs.

Split

  • Exactly one existing canonical asset remains plus a newly created canonical asset.
  • Available quota must be checked atomically.
  • Source-device bindings and evidence must be mapped to each asset.
  • Ambiguous records remain quarantined until reviewed.
  • Licensed count increases by one only after the split commits.

4.5 Technical invariants

These must always hold in implementation:

  • One canonical asset per unique monitored device.
  • A source attachment never changes asset count.
  • Quota changes occur only in one transaction.
  • Per-tenant usage cannot become negative.
  • Canonical UUID is never reused.
  • A source-device binding belongs to exactly one tenant.
  • An active source-device binding belongs to exactly one canonical asset.
  • Merge or split usage update is audited and reversible through history.
  • Source disconnection alone is not a permanent removal.
  • Pending and removed states do not silently masquerade as active assets.

4.6 Commercial policy decisions

The following are OWNER DECISION REQUIRED:

  • 30-day reactivation grace.
  • Whether pending identities reserve quota.
  • Whether deactivated assets reserve quota.
  • Whether reserved assets count as billable usage.
  • Immediate quota release exceptions.
  • Permanent removal authorization.
  • Pending identity quarantine duration.
  • Whether one-person or two-person removal/merge/split approval is required.

Reasonable alternative:

Choice Technical consequence Recommendation
Pending identity reserves quota Conservative admission; false positives can block new devices PROPOSED — reserve only for a short owner-approved period
Pending identity does not reserve quota False positive does not consume quota Accept pending as technical quarantine only
Deactivation frees slot immediately Re-enrollment can become expensive; easy to avoid stale billing Safer for strict current-usage billing
Deactivated asset has 30-day grace Retains reactivation and avoids churn PROPOSED — owner approval only
Reserved asset is billable Prevents slot reuse; may overcharge after disconnection Requires commercial approval
Reserved asset is non-billable Allows a grace reservation separately from licensed count PROPOSED — owner approval only

NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION: define four separate counters: active, reserved, pending and available quota. Do not use only one billable counter for all lifecycle states.

5. Workstream C: roadmap reconciliation

5.1 Original roadmap baseline

The approved original sequence remains:

  1. Core Platform
  2. Linux Agent and Data Ingestion
  3. Core Security Engine
  4. Vulnerability and Threat Intelligence
  5. Dashboard and Reporting
  6. External Integrations and Windows Agent
  7. MELIRA AI
  8. SOAR and Advanced Response
  9. Cross-Platform Agent
  10. Production Readiness

It must not be changed in this package.

5.3 Cross-platform options

Option A: retain original numbering

Keep Phases 1-10 unchanged and add architecture discovery as a pre-implementation gate.

Advantages:

  • Lowest commercial/documentation disruption.
  • Preserves owner-approved scope.
  • Platform work remains in original Phase 9.
  • Production phase remains original Phase 10.

Disadvantages:

  • Database, authorization and asset licensing foundations are not explicitly separated for dependency tracking.

Option B: revised dependency sequence

Use Revised Phases 0-10 from the current roadmap.

Advantages:

  • Security/identity prerequisites precede tenant data and AI.
  • Asset identity precedes broad Agent and integration work.
  • Work is easier to stage vertically.

Disadvantages:

  • Existing numbering changes materially.
  • Cross-platform platforms have no explicit destination.
  • Vulnerability and dashboard work are repositioned.

Option C: split platform delivery

Keep original phases as baseline and assign:

  • Linux Agent: original Phase 2, because it is the first operational Agent.
  • Windows Agent and external integrations: original Phase 6.
  • BSD/macOS: a proposed cross-platform Phase 9 subphase.
  • Android/iOS: a separate mobile subphase after permission and policy review.
  • Platform-specific monitoring and compatibility testing: inside each platform subphase and Phase 10.

This option increases test and schedule accuracy but requires explicit owner approval.

5.4 Recommended revised sequence

NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION: retain the original ten-phase numbering as the approved roadmap baseline. Add pre-implementation architecture gates without renumbering implementation phases.

PROPOSED — OWNER APPROVAL REQUIRED: for the revised sequence, place:

  • Architecture discovery before implementation.
  • Database and tenant authorization foundations in the Core Platform phase.
  • Linux Agent first.
  • BSD and macOS in original Cross-Platform Agent Phase 9 after Linux/Windows platform capability patterns mature.
  • Android and iOS in a platform subtrack inside original Phase 9, but only after OS permission, sandbox and privacy constraints are documented.
  • Compatibility testing for every platform as a phase exit criterion and again in Production Readiness.

Do not assume generic "cross-platform" coverage for mobile or desktop platforms.

PostgreSQL implementation readiness result: not ready for first migration. The team may begin narrow read-only architecture testing and schema spike work, but production migrations for asset, source binding and quota need the unresolved decisions and formal constraints above.

7. Security and concurrency risks

High-risk areas

  1. Cross-tenant source binding or fingerprint collision.
  2. Per-tenant counter oversubscription.
  3. Fingerprint key rotation creating duplicate canonical assets.
  4. Split/merge count drift.
  5. Migration retry creating duplicate aliases or lifecycle records.
  6. Interrupted migration leaving old/new aliases that disagree.
  7. RLS context leaking across pooled database connections.
  8. Administrator access bypassing tenant context.
  9. Source credentials accepted outside stable source-device binding.
  10. Raw source identifiers used in logs or indexes.

Required pre-migration checks

  • Tenant-inclusive foreign keys for every tenant-owned relationship.
  • Runtime database role cannot bypass RLS.
  • Identity and quota transactions use explicit tenant locks.
  • Fingerprint alias uniqueness cannot allow a data source to bind twice to conflicting assets.
  • Migration cursor is recoverable and idempotent.
  • Asset usage counter is reconciled against lifecycle state.
  • Merge/split operations are privileged and audited.
  • RPO, backup/restore and secret key recovery are documented.

8. Alternatives considered

Fingerprint storage alternatives

  1. Raw source identifier as unique key: rejected; privacy and migration risk.
  2. One fingerprint only, rotated in place: rejected; in-flight lookup can miss existing devices.
  3. Old and new aliases on the binding: recommended.
  4. Canonical asset ID derived from fingerprint: rejected; key rotation would invalidate identity.
  5. Probabilistic merge by IP/hostname: rejected as automatic licensing evidence.

Lifecycle alternatives

  1. No grace: simple but disruptive; OWNER DECISION REQUIRED.
  2. 30-day grace: recommended technical default for reactivation; PROPOSED — OWNER APPROVAL REQUIRED.
  3. Pending identity consumes quota: conservative but can block other registration; OWNER DECISION REQUIRED.
  4. Pending identity consumes no quota: safer for false positives but may encourage re-enrollment; NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION.

Roadmap alternatives

  1. Preserve original numbering: recommended if owner accepts only dependency refinements.
  2. Adopt revised numbered sequence: technically preferable for security dependencies, but owner approval is required.
  3. Split Linux/Windows/BSD/macOS/mobile agent tracks: best platform delivery accuracy, but increases roadmap and testing scope.

9. PostgreSQL example sequence

The following is a proposed transaction sequence only:

BEGIN;

SELECT *
FROM asset_tenant_license
WHERE tenant_id = $1
FOR UPDATE;

SELECT b.*
FROM source_device_binding b
JOIN source_device_fingerprint_alias f
  ON f.tenant_id = b.tenant_id
 AND f.binding_id = b.binding_id
WHERE f.tenant_id = $1
  AND f.data_source_id = $2
  AND f.fingerprint_digest = $3;

-- If no binding and registration is authoritative:
-- recheck identity aliases and quota;
-- create asset, binding and alias;
-- append lifecycle and license history;

COMMIT;

No DDL or migration is created by this package.

12. Final implementation status

  • NOT IMPLEMENTED: PostgreSQL, RLS, assets, source bindings, fingerprint migration or lifecycle enforcement.
  • NOT TESTED: concurrent registration, migration recovery, merge/split, restore or tenant isolation.
  • EXISTING APPROVED REQUIREMENT: Python backend, PostgreSQL primary database, external AI SaaS only, no local GPU, and one licensed asset per unique monitored device.
  • NEW TECHNICAL RECOMMENDATION: stable binding plus versioned fingerprint aliases; small resumable migration batches; tenant-row quota locking.
  • OWNER DECISION REQUIRED: roadmap numbering, cross-platform destinations, lifecycle grace, pending reservations and commercial billing semantics.
